clinicalPearls: Caused by usually de novo gain-of-function variants in CACNA1E, encoding the pore-forming alpha-1E subunit of the R-type voltage-gated calcium channel (Cav2.3).
Presents as a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE69) with early-onset refractory seizures, profound hypotonia and severe global developmental impairment.
Distinctive features in the most severe cases include a hyperkinetic or dyskinetic movement disorder, contractures or arthrogryposis, macrocephaly and central hypoventilation.
Recurrent variants cluster in functionally critical channel regions and enhance calcium influx by slowing channel inactivation, a gain-of-function mechanism.
It belongs to the calcium channelopathy family and should be distinguished from CACNA1A, CACNA1C (Timothy syndrome), CACNA1D and CACNA1H disorders.
Neuroimaging may show atrophy or be nonspecific, so the diagnosis is genetic.
Seizures are frequently pharmacoresistant, and care is supportive and multidisciplinary.
reference.pathophysiology: CACNA1E encodes the alpha-1E pore-forming subunit of Cav2.3, the R-type high-voltage-activated calcium channel enriched in neurons, where it contributes to calcium-dependent signalling, burst firing and neurotransmitter release. Recurrent de novo missense variants act through a gain-of-function mechanism, typically slowing channel inactivation and increasing calcium current, which drives neuronal hyperexcitability, epileptic encephalopathy and a movement disorder. The most severe outcomes, including contractures and central hypoventilation, are associated with the strongest functional effects on the channel. Inheritance is autosomal dominant and almost always de novo.
additionalDifferentials: CACNA1A disorders (Cav2.1 — epileptic encephalopathy, episodic ataxia, hemiplegic migraine)
CACNA1D disorders (Cav1.3 — aldosteronism with seizures and neurodevelopmental disorder)
STXBP1, KCNQ2, SCN2A and SCN8A developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
Other causes of arthrogryposis with neonatal encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: Trio exome or genome sequencing, or an epilepsy gene panel
EEG, which may show multifocal discharges, burst-suppression or other severe patterns
Brain MRI showing atrophy or nonspecific findings
Assessment of respiratory drive or a sleep study where hypoventilation is suspected
Parental testing to confirm de novo occurrence
redFlags: Neonatal or early-infantile refractory seizures with profound hypotonia
Central hypoventilation or unexplained respiratory insufficiency
Progressive contractures or arthrogryposis with a movement disorder
Developmental stagnation without acquisition of milestones
reference.prognosis: The gain-of-function end of the spectrum is severe, with refractory epilepsy, profound disability and a risk of early death, particularly where central hypoventilation occurs; milder phenotypes are described with lesser channel disturbance.
pitfalls: Treating it as a generic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy without recognising the calcium-channel mechanism and its movement-disorder and respiratory features.
Confusing it with other CACNA1-family disorders, which differ in channel and phenotype.
Overlooking central hypoventilation as a cause of clinical deterioration.
Expecting a diagnostic MRI, as imaging is often nonspecific.
management: Control the refractory seizures with antiseizure medication guided by the EEG pattern and seizure semiology.
Provide supportive care for profound hypotonia, including feeding support and secretion management.
Manage the hyperkinetic or dyskinetic movement disorder with appropriate movement-disorder pharmacotherapy.
Assess and support respiratory drive, providing ventilatory support where central hypoventilation occurs.
Address contractures and arthrogryposis with physiotherapy and orthopaedic input.
Coordinate multidisciplinary developmental support through paediatric neurology.
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and confirm de novo occurrence by parental testing.
Escalate promptly during respiratory compromise, recognising the risk of early death.
